THE DESOLATION OF THE DROUGHT

By: Este de Klerk | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
In just more than 20 days, taps in Bloemfontein, serving 2,5 million people, would have dried up completely. Live-stock in the FS and countrywide are dying and farmers say all they can do is pray.

Summary:
In just more than 20 days, taps in Bloemfontein, serving 2,5 million people, would have dried up completely. Smaller farming towns like Reddersburg are already fully dependable on water brought to them by the army, who has erected a big tent in the middle of town.
What was meant to be the beginning of the planting season and small green maize plants starting to rise from the ground, now looks like the Kalahari dessert. Massive dust storms are common in the Free State and the wind is whipping up the now loose earth from fields and turning it into banks of brown sand. Farmers here produce 44% of the country's maize and the Free State is called the bread-basket of the country. But it hasn't rained and when it did, it were a mere few drops.


Live-stock in the FS and countrywide are dying and farmers say all they can do is pray.

Further information:
It is the worst drought in four decades.
It is estimated that the country would at least need R900 million in relief and mitigation – money the country apparently doesn’t have to give in drought relief.

Kwazulu-Natal, the Free State and Limpopo have all been declared disaster areas. North West, the Northern Cape and Mpumalanga are also affected and monitored.

It will impact on livelihoods and drain the economy.

A source said that the money in the drought disaster kitty was given to Eskom to keep the lights in the country on till April/May this year. (need to confirm this)

The drought has been having a massive financial impact on farmers, with many struggling to meet their targets and making a loss.
Many farmers will be forced to rely on loans in order to continue farming – the key sector players are cash-strapped at the moment.

The Department of Agriculture has recently reported that the combined debt among farmers rose 14% last year to R117 billion.
Grain farmers use debt security as part of their operations, while live-stock breeders use government guarantees to make contingencies for the dry season.
The drought and poor rainfall will be forcing maize farmers of SA – Africa’s biggest corn producer – to reduce the 2016 season plantings to the smallest since 2011.
By June this year, credit extension to the industry was approaching R100-billion. Most of the debt is carried by the country’s major banks.

The worst-affected farmers are emerging ones, who do not have the capital and savings to survive the loss of consecutive harvests. Owing to land transfer issues – in many cases, the government has kept title deeds – several hundred thousand farmers are unable to get loans and insurance. Previous droughts have seen farmers that were already operating at a loss being forced to sell their property to pay back debts. This led to mass-layoffs of farmworkers.

The national drought is the worst in 23 years. The last two droughts coincided with El Nino weather patterns in the Pacific Ocean, which warms the world’s largest body of water and creates drought in much of the southern hemisphere. Its appearance in 1982 and 1991 led to two year-long droughts across South Africa.

Dry conditions last year cut South Africa’s maize crop by a third and the weather outlook and historic troughs for the rand drove prices for yellow maize, used for animal feed, to 2015 highs over 3000 rand per tonne last week.

In the short run, this may push down livestock and meat prices, but costlier maize, South Africa’s staple, will hurt poor households, while rural households will also suffer.

Live-stock farmers who haven’t made provision in feed for their animals, now have to auction them off or have them slaughtered – they simply cannot afford to pay R3000/ton for feed for their animals.

GOVN OFFERING DISASTER SUPPORT: While government did offer financial support, the R220 million offered in disaster management were only for upcoming live-stock farmers. Other live-stock farmers were urged by government to cut the size of their herds as drought conditions suck moisture out of grazing land.

Grain SA says that summer crops – soybeans, maize, sugarcane – and livestock farming are hardest hit. After drought last year, SA’s staple maize crop was cut by a third, but the situation looks much worse for the current planting season. Farmers cannot plant (latest to plant is always in December), because it hasn’t yet rained. The National Agricultural Marketing Council predicts more grain will have to be imported. Commercial farmers are expected to plant 2,5 million hectares of maize in 2016, 3,8% less than the last season.

Grain SA says the drought to date will cost farmers R10-billion in lost crops. With maize process increasing and food for humans prioritized, livestock farmers must spend R2-billion more to import grain for animals.
Grain SA says the price of maize – to import - will increase by a further quarter this summer – and this will have an ultimate affect on the consumer in escalated food prices.

The impact on average food prices is hidden in the size of the global food market. But quarterly statistics released by the agriculture department show that the price of maize in shops has already gone up by a third, due to the drought last summer.
In response to the drought, government has created a multi-departmental national drought task team.

The sugar-growing KZN, which had been declared a disaster area first of all the provinces, is the driest it has been in over a century, according to data provided by the South Africa Weather Service. Wool yields are set to fall dramatically this year and if it doesn’t rain soon, sheep farmers say they would have to sell their sheep at a steep discount. Last year’s drought contributed to this year’s stressed farmers – as animals didn’t breed properly. Mpumalanga contributes about 4,5 million kg of wool per year, or 10% of SA’s overall production.

For most parts in central, eastern, northern and western FS, it now looks like an arid Kalahari dessert.
The breadbasket of the country, the Free State produces 44% of the country’s maize.
The FS Agriculture Department only ONE percent of farmers in the province have reported that their fields are fit for grazing and planting.

WATER:

More than 2,7-million households are currently facing water shortages across the country. Increased feed costs, electricity used for irrigation and the threat of cheaper imported agricultural Consumers Countrywise will ultimately feel the impact. The CSIR said in October that temperatures across Africa were rising at twice the global average. Long-term predictions on rainfall are hard to make, but there is a high probability of dry conditions until at least April next year. This is bad news for farmers, because it means continuing, and probably, intensified drought. 2016 is the great unknown. If farmers have another season with low yields, there will be farmers that cannot survive the knack.

Government can do little besides mitigating the impact of the drought by enforcing water-saving measures and moving water between catchments. South Africa is already the 31st driest country in the world and relies on Lesotho’s Katse Dam to provide enough water for agriculture and industry in Gauteng, Mpumalanga and the Free State. In Limpopo and the North West – where agriculture is almost solely rain-fed – the only solution is rain.

The impact on the African region is much worse – South Africa’s neighbours are also experiencing an extended drought – water levels in the Zambezi River have dropped so low that Victoria Falls regularly stops flowing. The World Food Programme’s last bulletin said: “Significant drops in crop production are expected in southern parts of Zimbabwe, Malawi, Madagascar, Lesotho and South Africa, because of the uncharacteristically low rainfall being experienced in the region.” This was coupled with a steady drop in crop yields in the area over the past five years. South Africa’s 31% drop in maize production last summer was therefore a major problem for Southern Africa, it said. “This poses a serious cause for concern, as it might trigger higher food process in the short term and a food deficit in surrounding countries.

Some parts of South Africa have been experiencing water shortages with the drought heavily impacting on the country’s water resources. Earlier in November, Minister of Water and Sanitation, Nomvula Mokonyane said that “engagements were underway to allow the government to access water from the Zambezi via Zimbabwe to further guarantee supply in the Northern parts of the country. The government was also drawing water from neighbouring Lesotho to augment the country’s resources, especially Gauteng. Mokonyane, said more than 170 water schemes in the country are currently affected by the drought.

South Africa has about 1600 water schemes made up of dams of all sizes and Mokonyane said small dams have run completely dry.
She said the situation is the worst since the 1960’s.
The Minister has called on Municipalities across the country to encourage controlled water use.

Kwazulu-Natal in particular is facing the lowest water levels in nearly 33 years – mainly due to the drought.
In Mbombela in Mpumalanga, strict water restrictions remain in place after the Crocodile River, which supplies most of the water to farms and residential areas in the area, stopped flowing.

Agriculture Minister Senzeni Zokwana has urged the country to use water sparingly, adding that irrigation agriculture uses about 60% of the country’s water and domestic users claim 27% of water resources

Last week, Johannesburg and Pretoria imposed water restrictions on residents.
Minister Mokonyane said that an estimated 6500 stand-alone rural communities were currently experiencing water shortages and that this could increase to 11 000 rural communities if the drought continues, mostly in KwaZulu-Natal, Mpumalanga, Limpopo and Northwest.She said that in badly affected areas such as the northern parts of KZN, southern parts of Mpumalanga, and parts of Limpopo, North West and the Northern Cape, about 50% of local water shortage was problematic and could become critical if not managed carefully.

In the Free State, water restrictions are also in effect in the province’s biggest municipalities. The City of Johannesburg is now facing level two water restrictions and residents are warned not to water gardens, refill swimming pools or wash cars furing daylight. Johannesburg’s 4,4 million citizens primarily rely on water from the Vaal, Sterkfontein and Grootdraai dams.

Press Release:


Drought Shockwaves
Sixty percent of South Africa’s maize is produced in the Free State. This area is fundamental to food security, but the worst drought in three decades has gripped the nation and Bloemfontein is set to run out of water before Christmas. In Smithfield, in the southern Free State, taps dried up completely a few weeks ago. The State has committed to helping emerging farmers, but desperate commercial farmers say they are fighting a losing battle in the face of further heat waves and soaring costs. Carte Blanche calculates the true cost of the drought.


Script:


DROUGHT SCRIPT

PRODUCER: ESTé DE KLERK

For the first time ever, a major city – the Judicial Capital of South Africa – will likely run out of water before Christmas.
But it’s not only the 700-thousand people living in Bloemfontein who would be deprived of this basic human right.
It’s also the other 2,1 million residents of the Free State province.
All twenty municipalities – comprising 84 towns - in the central province of South Africa will be impacted.

Farmers are the hardest hit.
Crop farmers need between 60 and 100 millimetres of rain to plant, but weather forecasters say that substantial rain can only be expected in Autumn.

JOHN CHOPPER LINK: Sixty percent of South Africa’s grain is grown in the Free State. It’s been described as the country’s breadbasket, but right now it looks more like a wasteland.

At first sight, a layman wouldn’t know the difference between a good or a bad year just before planting time.
But it’s the water and moisture in the underground-soil that make all the difference, says Bultfontein maize farmer, Anton Botha.

These are images taken at Anton’s farm:
The beginning of the 2014-planting season: one of his workers knee-deep in water one and a half metres underground;
And this picture - taken on Friday: at a level of two and a half metres with no water or moisture in the ground.

One would think that drastic conditions call for drastic measures – but the pre-announced water shedding of between 9pm and 5am has not even been applied in Bloemfontein once this week.

Water restrictions in the Free State – and the country - are in place, including taking showers instead of baths, using “grey water” from baths or washing machines to flush toilets and only water your garden with a bucket, not a hose or irrigation system.

The Free State government says the police will strictly monitor water usage, says the province’s overall head of policy, planning, governance and strategic infrastructure, Thuso Ramaema.

JOHN: You seem to be the first province to say to your people that you must confront the possibility that one of these days your taps are going to run dry?

THUSO RAMAEMA: We are in a water crisis. If nothing happens and there’s no rain and groundwater are just not happening, we have to go to desalination processes, recycling processes.

The levels of fourteen of the province’s nineteen dams are below 60% and eight are under 20%.

THUSO RAMAEMA: The plan B is that we will have limited augmentation from the Lesotho Highlands watersystem.

JOHN LINK: This isn’t the first severe drought experienced by this country, but what makes this one different is it follows a long period of hot, dry weather. It is almost a drought on top of a drought and that makes the next few months and years extremely unpredictable.

Kwazulu-Natal is the driest it’s been in a century and time to plant there has sadly come and gone. It’s been declared a drought disaster area in December last year, followed by the North West in July, the Free State in September and Limpopo in November. Mpumalanga and the Western Cape are both at advanced stages of preparation for the declaration of disaster areas.

In Parliament earlier this month, President Jacob Zuma said government was monitoring how each province had been affected.

ANNETTE STEYN/DA MP: This drought could put South Africa in a food security crisis. Would you agree that we declare this as a national disaster?

PRESIDENT JACOB ZUMA: It has not declared it as a national disaster. When that moment comes, it would certainly do so.

JOHN LINK CHOPPER: South Africa’s agricultural sector had turned farming in low rainfall areas into a fine art, but growing anything during prolonged periods of drought, is nothing short of miraculous.

The hot weather conditions and poor rain fall are due to the 2015 El Nino – warming the Pacific Ocean, creating drought in much of the southern hemisphere.

Farmers don’t only have to contend with the erratic weather patterns, but also with the financial pressure a drought brings.

ANTON BOTHA: Ja, John, ek weet daar is baie boere wie se produksie-krediet ingetrek is, wat nie voluit kan produseer nie.

JOHN: Do you perceive many farmers going under?

ANTON BOTHA: ek dink nie daar is baie boere wat nog ‘n jaar kan oorleef in ons distrik nie. Ek weet van buur-distrikte waar reeds baie grond in die mark is.

Forty-six farms to be exact.
And the R226-million government provided in drought relief for emerging farmers, is a far cry from what’s needed to save the people who provide the country with food, says Grain SA CEO, Jannie de Villiers.

JANNIE DE VILLIERS: When we compare it to the '92 drought for instance I think government made something like 6.3 billion rand available at that time it was a lot of money and farmers got like R120 per hector you know irrespective of whether they had a crop or not just to make sure that you have got your food security capacity ready for the next season. What we have heard for this year the whole contingency was used for Eskom because of the crisis that they had and that there is actually very little available towards agriculture now that we have a problem with the drought.

And emerging farmer from the Wesselsbron-area, Israel Motlhabane, says government’s drought relief aid is too little, too late.

ISRAEL: My financial position it tells me, or informs me that maybe within 2 months I will be dry up.

Israel has already lost five cattle – three of which were cows that died while giving birth because they were just too weak.

In a good year, farmers deliver more than 12 million tons of maize – the bigger the shortfall, the more South Africa has to import.

JANNIE DE VILLIERS: If we are not going to receive rain and the heat is going to be terrible as predicted by some of these El Nino experts , then we could go as low as 8 million tons.

Which means we would have to import at least 2,5 million tons of maize.

(RAIN QUIETNESS FOR SECOND OR 3 BEFORE VO STARTS)

The sound we are all longing to hear.
More than 170 of the country’s 1600 water schemes are affected by the drought.
Several smaller dams have dried up completely.
One is in the water-stricken town of Smithfield in the Mokhare Municipality in the Free State.

JOHN LINK : In the distance, people used to sit over there and catch fish, those tress over there used to be on an island – but the worst drought in 23 years has changed it into this. That and no small measure of political incompetence.

It’s been more than a month since taps ran dry.
And for five days, aid from the local municipality was non-existent.
For the past three weeks, municipal and additional tankers have been delivering water to the school, hospital and township residents like Betty Ghadimane, who every day has to carry the heavy buckets of water on her head.

BETTY GHADIMANE: So dis is so bietjie ver, die 20kg wat ons dra, ons het nie lekker krag nie, so dis baie moeilik.

JOHN: Dis nie veel water nie. Is dit genoeg vir ‘n dag?

BETTY: Nee, Ntati, dis nie genoeg vir ‘n dag nie, want daar is by die 20 litre daar moet kos wees, ek moet opwas, dis baie min.

Smithfield’s main water source is the Caledon River, but the municipality also sources water from the local dam. The town, however has a rich underground water source and more than 12 boreholes have not been maintained, says Ian Riddle, DA councilor.

IAN RIDDLER: They are supposed to pump from the Caledon River and for over three years they didn’t pump from the Caledon River. So, all the water went past and they emptied this dam. By the time they got to the Caledon River, there was no more water left.

The Mokhare local municipality has been the first to call in the help of the South African National Defence Force.

We requested an interview with the municipality.
But the Municipal Manager, Thabo Panyani, who has to take responsibility for the water crisis and lack of maintenance, insisted we interview instead Danie Marais – a consultant who assists struggling municipalities on a contract-basis for the Free State Premier.

JOHN: How much of what we are dealing with in this particular municipality is a result of the drought and how much of it is a result of mismanagement?

DANIE MARAIS: The municipality didn’t have any control over the drought. Somebody referred to the boreholes which was not maintained. If you don’t use something or don’t need to maintain it, you….

JOHN: That seems a scandalous attitude for me, when you are in the centre of a maize producing area, not to take care of your borehole, is a dereliction of duty.

DANIE MARAIS: Definitely not in this municipality, where their main source is the Caldeon river. There is no control from the counsel’s side …

JOHN: But you just said they haven’t maintained their boreholes?

DANIE MARAIS: Since the dam and the river have been built, there was no need for it.

THUSO RAMAEMA: One would not quite want to say that the infrastructure was mismanaged, because it is a historical problem. Those boreholes have not been commissioned for quite a time. In some of the towns, the infrastructure has been there, but neglected.

IAN RIDDLER: There is 14 or 16 municipal boreholes. One of them down in the Poort, we believe have something like 80 000 litres of water an hour and they could have helped the situation.

DANIE MARAIS: Money to renew it or to upgrade or to maintain it is limited.

But there was enough money. R7,4 million set aside for infrastructure wasn’t spent in the last financial year.
And an additional 5,9-million allocated in June. But the first meeting about the issue was only held on October, the 15th. Less than two weeks later, taps ran dry.

DANIE MARAIS: It’s like a farmer. The farms are also declared disaster areas. But now they go to government and ask for assistance. Why didn’t they make provision? Now everybody is pointing fingers to the municipality, why didn’t you make provision, why didn’t you maintain the boreholes?

JOHN: The difference is the farmers did actually do everything that they could, they did maintain their boreholes, they did maintain their infrastructure. Questions are raised around whether municipalities have done likewise?

DANIE MARAIS: They did maintain the sources they do have.

The SANDF’s agreement with the local municipality ends tomorrow.
And even after all the help, there’s still no consistent running water in the town or the township.





PROMO’S

PROMO 1: 15”

NO VOICEOVER

JOHN LINK: What would happen when a city like Bloemfontein, with a population of 700 000 people run out of water? Well, that is a ……

PROMO 2: 15”

Water restrictions are in full effect, but will South Africans take it seriously?

THUSO: We’ll run out of water by the end of December if we are not careful.

PROMO 3: 10:
South Africa’s farming industry is threatened by the worst drought in 23 years. Add our current lack of water resources and you have a country in crisis.

Carte Blanche HD Nikola Vrahimis 04 December 2015 Press Release: Drought Shockwaves Sixty percent of South Africa’s maize is produced in the Free State. This area is fundamental to food security, but the worst drought in three decades has gripped the nation and Bloemfontein is set to run out of water before Christmas. In Smithfield, in the southern Free State, taps dried up completely a few weeks ago. The State has committed to helping emerging farmers, but desperate commercial farmers say they are fighting a losing battle in the face of further heat waves and soaring costs. Carte Blanche calculates the true cost of the drought. Script: DROUGHT SCRIPT PRODUCER: ESTé DE KLERK For the first time ever, a major city – the Judicial Capital of South Africa – will likely run out of water before Christmas. But it’s not only the 700-thousand people living in Bloemfontein who would be deprived of this basic human right. It’s also the other 2,1 million residents of the Free State province. All twenty municipalities – comprising 84 towns - in the central province of South Africa will be impacted. Farmers are the hardest hit. Crop farmers need between 60 and 100 millimetres of rain to plant, but weather forecasters say that substantial rain can only be expected in Autumn. JOHN CHOPPER LINK: Sixty percent of South Africa’s grain is grown in the Free State. It’s been described as the country’s breadbasket, but right now it looks more like a wasteland. At first sight, a layman wouldn’t know the difference between a good or a bad year just before planting time. But it’s the water and moisture in the underground-soil that make all the difference, says Bultfontein maize farmer, Anton Botha. These are images taken at Anton’s farm: The beginning of the 2014-planting season: one of his workers knee-deep in water one and a half metres underground; And this picture - taken on Friday: at a level of two and a half metres with no water or moisture in the ground. One would think that drastic conditions call for drastic measures – but the pre-announced water shedding of between 9pm and 5am has not even been applied in Bloemfontein once this week. Water restrictions in the Free State – and the country - are in place, including taking showers instead of baths, using “grey water” from baths or washing machines to flush toilets and only water your garden with a bucket, not a hose or irrigation system. The Free State government says the police will strictly monitor water usage, says the province’s overall head of policy, planning, governance and strategic infrastructure, Thuso Ramaema. JOHN: You seem to be the first province to say to your people that you must confront the possibility that one of these days your taps are going to run dry? THUSO RAMAEMA: We are in a water crisis. If nothing happens and there’s no rain and groundwater are just not happening, we have to go to desalination processes, recycling processes. The levels of fourteen of the province’s nineteen dams are below 60% and eight are under 20%. THUSO RAMAEMA: The plan B is that we will have limited augmentation from the Lesotho Highlands watersystem. JOHN LINK: This isn’t the first severe drought experienced by this country, but what makes this one different is it follows a long period of hot, dry weather. It is almost a drought on top of a drought and that makes the next few months and years extremely unpredictable. Kwazulu-Natal is the driest it’s been in a century and time to plant there has sadly come and gone. It’s been declared a drought disaster area in December last year, followed by the North West in July, the Free State in September and Limpopo in November. Mpumalanga and the Western Cape are both at advanced stages of preparation for the declaration of disaster areas. In Parliament earlier this month, President Jacob Zuma said government was monitoring how each province had been affected. ANNETTE STEYN/DA MP: This drought could put South Africa in a food security crisis. Would you agree that we declare this as a national disaster? PRESIDENT JACOB ZUMA: It has not declared it as a national disaster. When that moment comes, it would certainly do so. JOHN LINK CHOPPER: South Africa’s agricultural sector had turned farming in low rainfall areas into a fine art, but growing anything during prolonged periods of drought, is nothing short of miraculous. The hot weather conditions and poor rain fall are due to the 2015 El Nino – warming the Pacific Ocean, creating drought in much of the southern hemisphere. Farmers don’t only have to contend with the erratic weather patterns, but also with the financial pressure a drought brings. ANTON BOTHA: Ja, John, ek weet daar is baie boere wie se produksie-krediet ingetrek is, wat nie voluit kan produseer nie. JOHN: Do you perceive many farmers going under? ANTON BOTHA: ek dink nie daar is baie boere wat nog ‘n jaar kan oorleef in ons distrik nie. Ek weet van buur-distrikte waar reeds baie grond in die mark is. Forty-six farms to be exact. And the R226-million government provided in drought relief for emerging farmers, is a far cry from what’s needed to save the people who provide the country with food, says Grain SA CEO, Jannie de Villiers. JANNIE DE VILLIERS: When we compare it to the '92 drought for instance I think government made something like 6.3 billion rand available at that time it was a lot of money and farmers got like R120 per hector you know irrespective of whether they had a crop or not just to make sure that you have got your food security capacity ready for the next season. What we have heard for this year the whole contingency was used for Eskom because of the crisis that they had and that there is actually very little available towards agriculture now that we have a problem with the drought. And emerging farmer from the Wesselsbron-area, Israel Motlhabane, says government’s drought relief aid is too little, too late. ISRAEL: My financial position it tells me, or informs me that maybe within 2 months I will be dry up. Israel has already lost five cattle – three of which were cows that died while giving birth because they were just too weak. In a good year, farmers deliver more than 12 million tons of maize – the bigger the shortfall, the more South Africa has to import. JANNIE DE VILLIERS: If we are not going to receive rain and the heat is going to be terrible as predicted by some of these El Nino experts , then we could go as low as 8 million tons. Which means we would have to import at least 2,5 million tons of maize. (RAIN QUIETNESS FOR SECOND OR 3 BEFORE VO STARTS) The sound we are all longing to hear. More than 170 of the country’s 1600 water schemes are affected by the drought. Several smaller dams have dried up completely. One is in the water-stricken town of Smithfield in the Mokhare Municipality in the Free State. JOHN LINK : In the distance, people used to sit over there and catch fish, those tress over there used to be on an island – but the worst drought in 23 years has changed it into this. That and no small measure of political incompetence. It’s been more than a month since taps ran dry. And for five days, aid from the local municipality was non-existent. For the past three weeks, municipal and additional tankers have been delivering water to the school, hospital and township residents like Betty Ghadimane, who every day has to carry the heavy buckets of water on her head. BETTY GHADIMANE: So dis is so bietjie ver, die 20kg wat ons dra, ons het nie lekker krag nie, so dis baie moeilik. JOHN: Dis nie veel water nie. Is dit genoeg vir ‘n dag? BETTY: Nee, Ntati, dis nie genoeg vir ‘n dag nie, want daar is by die 20 litre daar moet kos wees, ek moet opwas, dis baie min. Smithfield’s main water source is the Caledon River, but the municipality also sources water from the local dam. The town, however has a rich underground water source and more than 12 boreholes have not been maintained, says Ian Riddle, DA councilor. IAN RIDDLER: They are supposed to pump from the Caledon River and for over three years they didn’t pump from the Caledon River. So, all the water went past and they emptied this dam. By the time they got to the Caledon River, there was no more water left. The Mokhare local municipality has been the first to call in the help of the South African National Defence Force. We requested an interview with the municipality. But the Municipal Manager, Thabo Panyani, who has to take responsibility for the water crisis and lack of maintenance, insisted we interview instead Danie Marais – a consultant who assists struggling municipalities on a contract-basis for the Free State Premier. JOHN: How much of what we are dealing with in this particular municipality is a result of the drought and how much of it is a result of mismanagement? DANIE MARAIS: The municipality didn’t have any control over the drought. Somebody referred to the boreholes which was not maintained. If you don’t use something or don’t need to maintain it, you…. JOHN: That seems a scandalous attitude for me, when you are in the centre of a maize producing area, not to take care of your borehole, is a dereliction of duty. DANIE MARAIS: Definitely not in this municipality, where their main source is the Caldeon river. There is no control from the counsel’s side … JOHN: But you just said they haven’t maintained their boreholes? DANIE MARAIS: Since the dam and the river have been built, there was no need for it. THUSO RAMAEMA: One would not quite want to say that the infrastructure was mismanaged, because it is a historical problem. Those boreholes have not been commissioned for quite a time. In some of the towns, the infrastructure has been there, but neglected. IAN RIDDLER: There is 14 or 16 municipal boreholes. One of them down in the Poort, we believe have something like 80 000 litres of water an hour and they could have helped the situation. DANIE MARAIS: Money to renew it or to upgrade or to maintain it is limited. But there was enough money. R7,4 million set aside for infrastructure wasn’t spent in the last financial year. And an additional 5,9-million allocated in June. But the first meeting about the issue was only held on October, the 15th. Less than two weeks later, taps ran dry. DANIE MARAIS: It’s like a farmer. The farms are also declared disaster areas. But now they go to government and ask for assistance. Why didn’t they make provision? Now everybody is pointing fingers to the municipality, why didn’t you make provision, why didn’t you maintain the boreholes? JOHN: The difference is the farmers did actually do everything that they could, they did maintain their boreholes, they did maintain their infrastructure. Questions are raised around whether municipalities have done likewise? DANIE MARAIS: They did maintain the sources they do have. The SANDF’s agreement with the local municipality ends tomorrow. And even after all the help, there’s still no consistent running water in the town or the township. PROMO’S PROMO 1: 15” NO VOICEOVER JOHN LINK: What would happen when a city like Bloemfontein, with a population of 700 000 people run out of water? Well, that is a …… PROMO 2: 15” Water restrictions are in full effect, but will South Africans take it seriously? THUSO: We’ll run out of water by the end of December if we are not careful. PROMO 3: 10: South Africa’s farming industry is threatened by the worst drought in 23 years. Add our current lack of water resources and you have a country in crisis.

metadata.Summary: In just more than 20 days, taps in Bloemfontein, serving 2,5 million people, would have dried up completely. Smaller farming towns like Reddersburg are already fully dependable on water brought to them by the army, who has erected a big tent in the middle of town. What was meant to be the beginning of the planting season and small green maize plants starting to rise from the ground, now looks like the Kalahari dessert. Massive dust storms are common in the Free State and the wind is whipping up the now loose earth from fields and turning it into banks of brown sand. Farmers here produce 44% of the country's maize and the Free State is called the bread-basket of the country. But it hasn't rained and when it did, it were a mere few drops. Live-stock in the FS and countrywide are dying and farmers say all they can do is pray.

It will impact on livelihoods and drain the economy. A source said that the money in the drought disaster kitty was given to Eskom to keep the lights in the country on till April/May this year. Many farmers will be forced to rely on loans in order to continue farming – the key sector players are cash-strapped at the moment. The Department of Agriculture has recently reported that the combined debt among farmers rose 14% last year to R117 billion. Grain farmers use debt security as part of their operations, while live-stock breeders use government guarantees to make contingencies for the dry season. Previous droughts have seen farmers that were already operating at a loss being forced to sell their property to pay back debts. This led to mass-layoffs of farmworkers. Its appearance in 1982 and 1991 led to two year-long droughts across South Africa. Live-stock farmers who haven’t made provision in feed for their animals, now have to auction them off or have them slaughtered – they simply cannot afford to pay R3000/ton for feed for their animals. The impact on average food prices is hidden in the size of the global food market.
